Chapter 6: Rediscovering Solitude in a Connected World.
Now that we've talked about setting boundaries, let's take things a step further and explore something that's almost become a lost art—solitude. And no, I don’t mean locking yourself away from everyone. What I’m talking about is freedom from the constant stream of input from other minds. Think of it as mental breathing room, where you get to process your own thoughts, reflect, and come up with ideas that are truly yours.
In today’s world, being alone with your thoughts is surprisingly rare. Most of us fill even the tiniest gaps in our day with podcasts, texts, or scrolling through social feeds. Ever notice how waiting in line or taking a short walk almost always turns into a chance to grab your phone? It’s almost automatic. But all that non-stop input? It leaves hardly any space for your mind to wander, pull things together, or just rest.
Here’s something to really think about—solitude isn’t just nice to have. It’s essential for your well-being and creativity. When you’re alone with your thoughts, you get a chance to examine what really matters to you, solve problems, and develop your own point of view. Without that space, you might find yourself feeling restless, anxious, or even a little disconnected from what you truly value.
So, how do you bring more solitude into your everyday life? Here are a few gentle ways to get started:
First, try embracing device-free moments. Let yourself have small pockets of the day where you don’t reach for your phone or any digital input. Maybe that means leaving your phone behind when you go for a walk, or while you’re cooking dinner. It can feel strange at first, but those moments add up.
Next, practice some reflective activities. Journaling, doodling, or even just sitting quietly can help you process what’s going on in your life and how you feel about it.
You can also set aside regular time for solo activities. Things like reading, hiking, or meditation are great ways to give yourself uninterrupted time to just be.
And here’s one more—limit the background noise. It’s so tempting to fill every silence with music, news, or conversation. But sometimes, letting things be quiet is exactly what your mind needs to settle and recharge.
This isn’t just theory. Let me give you a couple of real-life examples. Imagine a teacher who starts taking her morning walks without headphones. Soon, she notices fresh ideas popping up for her lesson plans. Or think about an entrepreneur who spends quiet evenings alone, and suddenly those tricky business challenges start to look a lot more manageable.
Now, I won’t pretend solitude always feels comfortable in the beginning. Without distractions, you might bump into boredom or even some tough emotions. But with a little practice, those moments turn into real opportunities—for growth, for insight, and for understanding yourself better.
When you make solitude a regular part of your life, it gets a lot easier to resist the constant pull of digital input. You’ll find more space for deeper relationships, clearer thinking, and a much stronger sense of who you really are.
